hints: Think of the thick dark liquid mixture pumped from underground that refineries process to get petrol, diesel and other fractions.
Recall how a fractionating column separates a mixture of liquids with different volatilities without chemical reaction.
walkthrough:
Name the natural store of hydrocarbons**
You are looking for the naturally occurring mixture that contains thousands of different alkanes, cycloalkanes and aromatics. That is crude oil, also called petroleum. It is formed over millions of years and is the feedstock for the petrochemical industry.

Link separation to a physical property**
These hydrocarbons are not separated by reacting them, they are separated physically. Each hydrocarbon has a different chain length and therefore a different boiling point. In fractional distillation the oil is vaporised and passed up a fractionating column where fractions condense at different levels according to their boiling points.

Final answer: name of source: crude oil / petroleum
outline of separation: separation / fractional distillation according to different boiling points.

hints: Recall the name for breaking long chain alkanes into shorter alkanes and alkenes by strong heating without air.
walkthrough:
Recognise breaking down by heat alone**
You heat a large alkane strongly with no oxygen, so it cannot be combustion. The long chain splits into smaller molecules, typically a shorter alkane plus an alkene. That breakdown process is called cracking.

hints: Count C and H atoms on the right for hexane plus butane plus ethene, then balance the number of heptane molecules on the left to match.
walkthrough:
Balance atoms, not just molecules**
Write the skeleton with heptane on the left and hexane, butane and ethene on the right. Count: right side has $6+4+2 = 12$ carbons if you use one ethene, but one heptane has only $7$ carbons. Try $2$ heptanes on the left, that gives $\text{C}_{14}\text{H}_{32}$. On the right $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14} + \text{C}_4\text{H}_{10} + 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ gives $\text{C}_{14}$ and $\text{H}_{14+10+8}=\text{H}_{32}$. So the balanced equation is $$2\text{C}_7\text{H}_{16} \rightarrow \text{C}_4\text{H}_{10} + \text{C}_6\text{H}_{14} + 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$$

hints: Start by converting 1.00 g of ethene to moles using $M_r$ of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 = 28.0$.
Use the equation $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 + 3\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ to relate moles of ethene to moles of $\text{CO}_2$.
Recall how to convert moles of gas to volume at room temperature and pressure using $24 \text{ dm}^3 \text{ mol}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Convert mass of ethene to moles**
Moles is the bridge for every gas calculation. $$\text{moles} = \frac{\text{mass}}{M_r}$$ For ethene, $M_r = (2 \times 12.0)+(4 \times 1.0) = 28.0$. So $$\text{moles C}_2\text{H}_4 = \frac{1.00}{28.0} = 0.0357 \text{ mol}$$

Apply the 1 to 2 ratio**
Look at the equation: $1$ mole of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ makes $2$ moles of $\text{CO}_2$. So simply double: $$\text{moles CO}_2 = 2 \times 0.0357 = 0.0714 \text{ mol}$$

Change moles of gas to volume at rtp**
At room temperature and pressure one mole of any gas occupies $24.0 \text{ dm}^3$. $$\text{volume} = \text{moles} \times 24.0$$ $$V = 0.0714 \times 24.0 = 1.71 \text{ dm}^3$$ Keep three significant figures to match the $1.00 \text{ g}$ data.

Final answer: moles $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 = 1.00/28.0 = 0.0357 \text{ mol}$
moles $\text{CO}_2 = 2 \times 0.0357 = 0.0714 \text{ mol}$
volume $\text{CO}_2 = 0.0714 \times 24.0 = 1.71 \text{ dm}^3$

hints: Think about what makes $\cdot\text{Cl}$ so reactive, focusing on its outer shell electron count.
walkthrough:
Picture the reactive particle**
A free radical is not an ion, it has no charge. It is a neutral atom or group with one electron sitting on its own in an orbital. For $\cdot\text{Cl}$ that single unpaired electron makes it desperate to pair up, which is why it is so reactive.
Final answer: species with an unpaired electron(s).

hints: Recall the name for bond breaking where the shared pair splits evenly, one electron to each atom.
Describe where the two electrons from the $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond end up to give two $\cdot\text{Cl}$ radicals.
walkthrough:
Name the even split**
When $\text{Cl-Cl}$ breaks to give two identical radicals, the bond pair cannot go to one side only. It splits evenly, one electron each way. That is called homolytic fission. Homo means same, lytic means breaking.

Track the electrons**
In $\text{Cl}_2$ the two chlorines share a pair. On homolytic fission that pair is shared out equally, so each $\text{Cl}$ keeps one electron and becomes $\cdot\text{Cl}$ with an unpaired electron. This needs UV light to supply the energy.

Final answer: homolytic fission / homolysis
the covalent electron pair is split equally, one electron goes to each chlorine atom.

hints: Remember the three stages initiation, propagation and termination, and think which one keeps radicals going by reacting a radical with a molecule.
walkthrough:
Place it in the chain**
Initiation made the first $\cdot\text{Cl}$. Now $\cdot\text{Cl}$ attacks $\text{CH}_4$ and makes a new radical $\cdot\text{CH}_3$. Because a radical is used up but a new radical is created, the chain continues. That chain carrying stage is propagation.

hints: Think about H abstraction: $\cdot\text{Cl}$ removes one H from methane, forming $\text{HCl}$ and leaving a carbon centred radical.
walkthrough:
Complete the H transfer**
The $\cdot\text{Cl}$ pulls one H atom off methane. The H joins Cl to make $\text{HCl}$, and methane is left as $\cdot\text{CH}_3$, the methyl radical. So $$\text{CH}_4 + \cdot\text{Cl} \rightarrow \cdot\text{CH}_3 + \text{HCl}$$ Notice the dot is now on carbon, ready for the next propagation step.

hints: Compare bonding in alkanes which have only single bonds with alkenes which have a $\text{C=C}$ double bond made of two different components.
Think about what an electrophile is attracted to and which part of the double bond provides exposed high electron density.
walkthrough:
Sort out the bond types**
In an alkane every C-C and C-H bond is a $\sigma$ bond, formed by direct head on overlap on the bond axis. It is strong and the electrons are held tightly between the nuclei. In an alkene the $\text{C=C}$ is made of one $\sigma$ bond plus one $\pi$ bond, where p orbitals overlap sideways above and below the axis.

Explain the electrophile attraction**
An electrophile loves electrons. The $\pi$ electrons stick out above and below the molecule and are held less tightly, so they are easily donated to an electrophile. Alkanes have no $\pi$ electrons to offer, only strong low energy $\sigma$ electrons, so they do not attract electrophiles and do not undergo electrophilic addition.

Final answer: alkanes contain only $\sigma$ bonds, alkenes contain $\sigma$ and $\pi$ bonds ($\text{C=C}$ is $\sigma + \pi$).
electrophiles are attracted to / attacked by the exposed electrons in the $\pi$ bond, so alkenes react with electrophiles but alkanes do not.
